analysis.one_liner: Requires newsprint makers and importers to recycle a rising share of newsprint each year.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 44 House members from both parties, never left committee and never got a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced companies that make or import newsprint to recycle a share of it each year, starting at no less than 20 percent and rising two percentage points a year for ten years. Companies could comply by de-inking old newspaper, buying recycled newsprint, or buying recycling credits from recyclers. The goal was to create steady demand for old newspapers, which were piling up because communities collect more than the market wants to buy.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities and taxpayers who pay to collect and landfill old newspapers: the bill's own findings said 90 percent of old newspaper waste was not recycled and that disposal costs communities $20 to $60 per ton. Recyclers who invest in de-inking facilities would gain a guaranteed market. The environment gains from reduced landfill volume.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities paying to bury old newspapers

how_it_helps.text: The bill required producers and importers of newsprint to recycle at least 20 percent of their annual output, rising two points a year for ten years, to create demand for old newspaper waste [S2][S3].

The bill's findings state that 90 percent of old newspaper waste in the U.S. was not recycled, that the market price for it collapsed from $30 a ton to a loss of $10 a ton, and that disposal costs communities between $20 and $60 a ton [S3].
Companies could comply by recycling through de-inking, buying recycled newsprint, or purchasing recycling credits, giving recyclers a market to invest in de-inking facilities [S2][S3].
The bill authorized $1.2 million for EPA staffing to run the recycling credit and tracking system [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Newsprint producers and importers, who would bear the cost of recycling, buying recycled content, or purchasing credits, and face civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation. Some of that cost would likely pass to newspapers and readers through newsprint prices.

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs would fall on newsprint producers and importers, and higher newsprint prices would flow through to newspaper publishers and ultimately readers [S3].
The bill added federal paperwork: producers, importers, and recyclers would have to keep two years of records and report quantities and prices to EPA quarterly and annually [S3].

The credit-trading system and the administrator-set recycling percentage added regulatory complexity, and the bill directed the administrator to consider extending similar mandates to high-grade office papers after six years [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but narrow: a recycling mandate on one product line, with flexible compliance options including a credit market to keep costs down. The benefit falls on communities and landfills, which the bill's own findings put at $20 to $60 per ton of disposal cost against recycling. On balance a modest, targeted bill whose costs fall on a specific industry and whose benefits are broadly spread.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Esteban Edward Torres introduced the bill on April 22, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials on April 30, 1993, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill drew 44 cosponsors, 37 Democrats and 7 Republicans, but never received a vote in either chamber [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Newsprint producers and importers avoided recycling mandates and compliance costs, while communities kept paying to landfill old newspapers that could have been recycled.

sides.party_line_note: All 44 cosponsors were House members, 37 Democrats and 7 Republicans, so sponsorship crossed party lines; the record shows no votes on the bill, so the floor split is unknown.

industries.note: They would have had to recycle at least 20 percent of their annual output, buy recycled content or credits, keep records, and face civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation. Compliance costs would likely pass through to publishers and readers.

A guaranteed and rising demand for old newspapers, plus a credit market they could sell into, would give recyclers stable revenue to invest in de-inking capacity. Communities benefit from the same demand because collected newspaper finds a buyer.

Publishers would likely pay more for newsprint if producers' compliance costs passed through, but they would also gain from stable recycling markets for the old papers their readers set out at the curb.

Communities pay $20 to $60 a ton to dispose of old newspapers under the current system; shifting that material to recycling cuts their disposal burden, though landfill operators would lose the volume.
